title: Uwais al-Qarni
subtitle: The man the Prophet ﷺ described although they never met
sources: Sahih Muslim 2542 — Umar relays the Prophet's ﷺ description of Uwais and the advice to ask him to seek forgiveness

chapters.heading: No One Took His Picture
chapters.body: Uwais ibn Amir of Qarn in Yemen is known to us through reports of Umar. Umar relayed that the Prophet ﷺ said that a man called Uwais would come to them from Yemen, from Qaran, a branch of Murad; he would leave no one in Yemen except his mother; he had leprosy, he prayed to Allah and it was cured except for a spot the size of a dinar or a dirham; his treatment of his mother would be excellent, and if he took an oath in Allah's name Allah would honour it. The Prophet ﷺ said: whoever among you meets him, ask him to seek forgiveness for you (Muslim 2542). When Umar met him he asked him to seek forgiveness for him, and he did (Muslim 2542). The greatest publicity Uwais ever received was a few sentences from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The sources tell us of his good treatment of his mother; the card adds nothing more about his life.

familyQuestion: Uwais became known through his care for his mother. Who is the unsung servant of a parent in your own family?

title: Jurayj the Worshipper
subtitle: A mother's call, a false accusation, and a baby who spoke
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3436 — the narration of Jurayj and the infant who spoke (Abu Hurayrah)
Qur'an 71:28 — 'my Lord, forgive me and my parents'

chapters.heading: The Voice That Broke the Ceiling
chapters.body: Jurayj was a worshipper in his hermitage, praying, when his mother called him. He wondered within himself — my mother or my prayer? — and kept praying. She asked Allah not to let him die until he had seen the faces of prostitutes. Later a woman tried to seduce him and he refused; she went to a shepherd, bore a boy, and claimed that Jurayj was the father. The people broke down his hermitage, pulled him out and insulted him. He did wudu, prayed, then went to the baby and asked: who is your father? — and the infant answered: the shepherd (Bukhari 3436). When the people said they would rebuild his hermitage of gold, he said: no, of nothing but mud. The Prophet ﷺ opened the report by saying that none spoke in the cradle but three, and Jurayj's story is the second of them (Bukhari 3436). The report is often read as a lesson on how heavily a parent's call weighs; how it applies in a particular case is a question for a scholar.

familyQuestion: His mother's call outranked his prayer. When your parent calls and you're busy — what wins?

title: The Three Men Trapped in the Cave
subtitle: A rock the size of a tent, three honest deeds, and one narrow door
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2215 — the full narration (Ibn Umar)

chapters.heading: The Rock That Rolled for Honesty
chapters.body: Three men were walking when rain began to fall and they entered a cave in a mountain; a big rock rolled down and blocked its mouth, and they said to each other: invoke Allah with the best deed you have done. The first said: my parents were old, and I would bring them milk before my family and children drank. One night I came late and found them asleep; I would not wake them, and my children cried at my feet until dawn — so O Allah, if I did that for You, relieve us. And the rock moved a bit. The second said: I loved a cousin of mine, the deepest love a man can have for a woman; she said I would not get my desire unless I paid her a hundred dinars; I saved until I had it, and when I was about to have her she said: fear Allah and do not break the seal except by right — and I stood up and left her. If I did that for You, relieve us. Two thirds of the rock was removed. The third said: I hired a worker for a faraq (three sa's) of millet; he refused to take it, so I sowed it and from its yield bought cows and a shepherd. After a time he came for his money, and I told him: go to those cows and the shepherd and take them, they are yours; he asked whether I was joking and I said I was not. If I did that for You, relieve us. And the rock was removed completely (Bukhari 2215). Each man asks Allah to remove the rock by the deed he did for His sake.

familyQuestion: Each man named a deed done only for Allah. What deed of yours is done for His sake alone?

title: The Man Who Killed 99
subtitle: The road to repentance, as the hadith tells it
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3470 — the narration (Abu Sa'id al-Khudri)
Sahih Muslim 2766 — the fuller narration, with the scholar's answer (Abu Sa'id al-Khudri)
Qur'an 4:100 — 'And whoever emigrates for the cause of Allah will find on the earth many [alternative] locations and abundance'

chapters.heading: One Hundred Minus One
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ said that among the Children of Israel there was a man who had killed ninety-nine people. He set out asking whether his repentance could be accepted, and came to a monk, who said no; so he killed him too (Bukhari 3470). In Muslim's fuller narration he then asked about the most knowledgeable person on earth and was directed to a scholar, who told him that yes, nothing stands between him and repentance, and that he should leave his evil land for a land where people worship Allah (Muslim 2766). On the way death came to him. The angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed over him; Allah ordered the village he was heading to to draw closer and the village he came from to draw away, and told the angels to measure; he was found one span closer to the village he was heading to, and he was forgiven (Bukhari 3470). The report says he turned his chest toward it as he died. A sinner's worst move is to close the door himself.

familyQuestion: The man set out for a land of worship and died on the way, and Allah accepted the intention. What step toward Allah are you postponing?

title: The Prostitute's Thirst
subtitle: A dog, a well, a shoe, and forgiveness wider than the sin
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3467 — the Israelite prostitute and the dog (Abu Hurayrah)
Qur'an 99:7-8 — 'whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it'

chapters.heading: She Gave a Dog Water
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ said that while a dog was going round a well, about to die of thirst, an Israelite prostitute saw it, took off her shoe and watered it, and Allah forgave her because of that (Bukhari 3467). The report says she was forgiven; it does not say what became of the rest of her life. A reflection: it shows that no act of mercy is too small to be seen, as the Qur'an says: 'whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it' (99:7).

familyQuestion: One act of water erased a lifetime's ledger. What small mercy are you dismissing as 'too small to count'?

title: Barsisa: A Tale We Cannot Verify
subtitle: The Qur'an's parable of Shaytan, and a monk's tale this app does not retell
sources: Qur'an 59:16-17 — 'like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve"'
Qur'an 14:22 — Shaytan on the Day of Judgment: 'I had no authority over you except that I invited you and you responded to me'
Not from the Qur'an and not an authentic hadith: a tale of a monk named Barsisa is retold in some commentaries on 59:16 — its details were not verified for this app (scholar review needed)

chapters.heading: What the Qur'an Says
chapters.body: Some commentaries retell a tale of a long-worshipping monk named Barsisa when explaining the parable in Surah al-Hashr: 'like the example of Satan' (59:16), who tells man to disbelieve and then disowns him. That tale is not from the Qur'an and not from an authentic hadith, and its details were not verified for this app, so it is not retold here. What the Qur'an itself gives is the parable and the sentence Shaytan will say when the matter is decided: 'I had no authority over you except that I invited you and you responded to me. So do not blame me; but blame yourselves' (14:22). The lesson that stands without the tale is the Qur'an's own: Shaytan invites, he does not compel, and on the Day he disowns those who followed him.

familyQuestion: Shaytan invites and does not compel. What invitation have you been treating as a command?

title: The Boy and the King
subtitle: The trench that burned for the believers, and the boy who named his Lord
sources: Sahih Muslim 3005 — the hadith of the king, the sorcerer, the monk and the boy (Suhaib)
Qur'an 85:4-10 — the companions of the trench

chapters.heading: Kill Me With the Others
chapters.body: Suhaib reported that the Prophet ﷺ said there was a king before you who had a magician. When the magician grew old he asked the king for a boy to teach, and on his way to the magician the boy met a monk and was impressed by his talk. When a huge beast blocked the road, the boy prayed that if the monk's affair was dearer to Allah than the magician's, the beast be killed, and threw a stone and killed it. He then began to cure the blind and the lepers. A blind courtier of the king came to him; the boy said, 'I do not cure anyone; it is Allah who cures,' the courtier believed and was cured. When the king asked who restored his sight and he said, 'My Lord,' the king said, 'Do you have a Lord besides me?' The king tortured them until the boy and the monk were named; the monk and the courtier were sawn in two rather than renounce their faith. The boy was taken up a mountain to be thrown down and the mountain quaked and his guards fell; he was taken in a boat to the middle of the sea and the boat capsized and they drowned. Then he told the king: gather the people on a plain, tie me to the trunk, take an arrow from my quiver and say 'In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy', and shoot. The king did, the arrow struck the boy's temple and he died, and the people said, 'We believe in the Lord of the boy.' The king ordered ditches dug and fires lit, and the people were told to renounce their religion or be thrown in; a woman with a baby hesitated, and the baby said: 'O mother, endure, for it is the truth' (Muslim 3005). The Qur'an speaks of the companions of the trench in Surah al-Buruj: 'those who have tortured the believing men and believing women and then have not repented will have the punishment of Hell' (85:10); the hadith itself does not say that the surah was revealed about this account.

familyQuestion: A baby told its mother to be patient. Who has encouraged you to stay on the truth when it was hard?

title: The Man from the Far End of the City
subtitle: One voice against a city — the Qur'an's own tale of the lonely caller
sources: Qur'an 36:20-30 — Surah Ya-Sin, the man from the far end of the city

chapters.heading: Follow the Messengers
chapters.body: The Qur'an tells it without a name: a man came running from the far end of the city — 'O my people, follow the messengers. Follow those who do not ask of you [any] payment, and they are [rightly] guided' (36:20-21). His words: 'I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me' (36:25). Then: 'It was said, Enter Paradise. He said, I wish my people could know Of how my Lord has forgiven me and placed me among the honored' (36:26-27). The verses then say: 'We did not send down upon his people after him any soldiers from the heaven, nor would We have done so. It was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished' (36:28-29). The Qur'an does not name the man or the city, and does not say how he died; commentators have offered reports, and this card follows the verses.

familyQuestion: He asked no payment of anyone and called people to follow the messengers. What are you doing that asks no reward from anyone but Allah?

title: Umar and the Pot of Milk
subtitle: A report that the caliph made himself vomit milk from the zakat camels
sources: Muwatta Malik, Book 17 (Zakat), no. 29 (Yahya's recension) — Zayd ibn Aslam: Umar drank milk, asked where it came from, and made himself vomit
Sahih al-Bukhari 3842 — Abu Bakr made himself vomit food that had come from fortune-telling (Aisha)
The report in the Muwatta reaches us through Zayd ibn Aslam, of the generation after Umar, without naming the person he heard it from; it is a report, not a chain to a witness (scholar review needed)

chapters.heading: The Milk He Gave Back
chapters.body: Zayd ibn Aslam reported that Umar ibn al-Khattab drank some milk that he liked very much and asked the man who had given it to him where it came from. The man said he had come to a watering-place and found grazing livestock from the zakat there, and was given some of their milk, which he put in his water-skin. Umar then put his hand in his mouth to make himself vomit (Muwatta Malik, Book 17, no. 29). Aisha reported something similar about Abu Bakr, in Bukhari: his slave gave him food, and when Abu Bakr learned that it had come from fortune-telling the slave had done in the days of ignorance, he put his hand in his throat and made himself vomit everything in his stomach (Bukhari 3842). Both reports are about being careful with what enters the body, and with the right of the poor in the zakat. The Muwatta report is not narrated by a witness, so this card calls it a report. Stories of Umar's night walks and a woman boiling stones for her children are not retold here because their sources were not checked.

familyQuestion: Umar gave back even milk that he had received innocently, because it belonged to the zakat. What are you holding that you should check the source of?

title: Khalid's Last Letter
subtitle: 'There is no part of me but bears the mark' — a commander who died in bed
sources: Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghaba fi Ma'rifat al-Sahaba (al-Ilmiyya ed., shamela.ws/book/1110), vol. 2 p. 143, no. 1399, Khalid ibn al-Walid — his words on his deathbed (read; not from the six books; Scholar review needed)
Qur'an 8:17 — 'And you threw not, [O Muhammad], when you threw, but it was Allah who threw'

chapters.heading: The Scars Were His Proof
chapters.body: Ibn al-Athir's entry on Khalid ibn al-Walid (Usd al-Ghaba, vol. 2 p. 143) reports that when death came to Khalid he said: "I have taken part in a hundred battles or about that many, and there is no span of my body without a blow, a stab or an arrow wound in it; and here I am dying on my bed as the ʿayr dies (the word is the donkey's) — so may the eyes of the cowards never sleep." The report is given in his own voice with no chain on that page. The same entry says he died at Homs in Syria, and also mentions another report that he died in Madinah in 21 AH, in the caliphate of Umar. This page does not mention his dismissal by Umar, his title 'Sword of Allah', or that he never lost a battle; those are not claimed here. As a reflection: he took the bed as a lack; the tradition may read the same scars as a debt paid.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He wept for dying in bed. What 'battle' are you wishing for while avoiding the one in front of you?

title: The Two Brothers and the Crow
subtitle: The first burial in history taught by a bird
sources: Qur'an 5:27-31 — the story of the two sons of Adam
Sahih al-Bukhari 1315 — the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to hurry with the funeral (Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: The First Burial
chapters.body: The Qur'an tells of the two sons of Adam who offered a sacrifice: 'it was accepted from one of them but was not accepted from the other.' Said the latter, 'I will surely kill you.' The former answered: 'Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous [who fear Him]. If you should raise your hand against me to kill me - I shall not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds' (5:27-28). His soul permitted to him the murder of his brother, so he killed him and became among the losers (5:30). Then 'Allah sent a crow searching in the ground to show him how to hide the disgrace of his brother. He said, O woe to me! Have I failed to be like this crow and hide the body of my brother?' And he became of the regretful (5:31). The Prophet ﷺ later taught his community to hurry with the funeral (Bukhari 1315).

familyQuestion: The Qur'an records the dead being covered, and the Prophet ﷺ taught us to hurry with the funeral. When did you last attend a funeral?

title: The Sleepers of the Cave
subtitle: They slept through an empire — and woke to find their Lord had kept their argument

chapters.heading: Young Men and Their People
chapters.body: The Qur'an tells of young men who 'believed in their Lord' and 'We increased them in guidance' (18:13). Their people had taken gods other than Allah, and they said so: 'These, our people, have taken besides Him deities' (18:15). The Qur'an calls the whole story 'among Our signs, a wonder' (18:9).

chapters.heading: The Sleep of Centuries
chapters.body: They took refuge in a cave: 'So We cast [a cover of sleep] over their ears within the cave for a number of years' (18:11). The Qur'an says: 'And they remained in their cave for three hundred years and exceeded by nine' (18:25). Their dog stretched its forelegs at the entrance (18:18). The Qur'an says people differ about how many they were and that Allah knows best their number (18:22).

chapters.heading: Waking
chapters.body: When they woke, they thought they had remained a day or part of a day; they said, 'Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained,' and sent one of them to the city with a silver coin (18:19). They feared that if their people came to know of them they would stone them or return them to their religion (18:20). The Qur'an says Allah caused them to be found 'that they would know that the promise of Allah is truth and that of the Hour there is no doubt'; and when the people disputed about them, some said 'construct over them a structure; their Lord is most knowing about them,' and those who prevailed said 'we will surely take over them a masjid' (18:21).

familyQuestion: They were found so that people would know the promise of Allah is true. What do you hold to that is true even when most people around you disagree?

title: The Two Gardens
subtitle: A rich man walked his perfect orchard and lost everything in one afternoon

chapters.heading: The Garden Walk
chapters.body: Two men — one given two gardens of grapes, ringed with palm trees, crops between, a river running through — walked among his wealth and said: 'I do not think that this will perish' (18:35). His companion, poor in gardens, answered: 'Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust and then from a sperm-drop and then proportioned you [as] a man?' (18:37). The Qur'an stages this conversation between the two men.

chapters.heading: The Arithmetic of More
chapters.body: The rich man kept counting: more wealth, more sons, more strength than his rival. 'even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return' (18:36) — he assumed he would fare well there too. His friend replied: 'It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden' (18:40).

chapters.heading: The Garden Encompassed
chapters.body: Then 'his fruits were encompassed [by ruin]' (18:42) — the verse does not say how; the poor man had spoken of 'a calamity from the sky' (18:40) — and he stood turning his hands over in dismay at what he had spent on it: 'I wish I had not associated with my Lord anyone' (18:42). All that remained was the sentence he had refused to say. The story ends with the truth both men now agreed on: 'Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope' (18:46). The verse puts the worth of wealth and children in its place and points to enduring good deeds.

familyQuestion: Which of our 'gardens' would we grieve losing — and what enduring deeds are we planting this month?

title: Dhul-Qarnayn: Power Held in Trust
subtitle: A ruler the Qur'an describes in sixteen verses and never names beyond his title
sources: Qur'an 18:83-98 — the report of Dhul-Qarnayn
Who he was is disputed in the sources; see Go deeper

chapters.heading: A Report, Not a Biography
chapters.body: They asked the Prophet ﷺ about Dhul-Qarnayn, and the answer begins with a promise of limits: 'I will recite to you about him a report' (18:83). Not his life, not his birth, not his country. The Qur'an says that Allah 'established him upon the earth' and 'gave him to everything a way' (18:84). The verses give a title and a trust, and leave the rest of the biography unspoken. Who he was is a question on which the scholars differ; the Go deeper section lays out their views without choosing for you.

chapters.heading: Three Roads
chapters.body: 'So he followed a way' (18:85). Reaching the setting of the sun, he 'found it [as if] setting in a spring of dark mud' (18:86) — the words say how it looked to him — and found a people there. Allah's words to him: either punish them or 'adopt among them [a way of] goodness'. His answer is the heart of the story: whoever does wrong we will punish, and then he is returned to his Lord; whoever believes and does righteousness will have 'a reward of Paradise', and 'we will speak to him from our command with ease' (18:87-88). Then another way, to the rising of the sun, where he found a people 'for whom We had not made against it any shield' (18:89-90). The verse closes with a line about knowledge: Allah had 'encompassed [all] that he had in knowledge' (18:91).

chapters.heading: The Dam
chapters.body: A third way brought him 'between two mountains', to a people who 'could hardly understand [his] speech' (18:92-93). They asked for help against Gog and Magog, 'corrupters in the land', and offered payment. He declined the offer: 'That in which my Lord has established me is better', and asked only for strength from them (18:94-95). 'Bring me sheets of iron'; then 'Blow [with bellows]'; then 'Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper' (18:96). Gog and Magog 'were unable to pass over it, nor ... to effect in it any penetration' (18:97). And what does he say of his own work? 'This is a mercy from my Lord; but when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level' (18:98). A ruler builds the most famous wall in the Qur'an, and credits it to mercy and calls it temporary.

familyQuestion: Dhul-Qarnayn said of what he built, 'This is a mercy from my Lord.' What do we have power over, even a little, and how could we use it as a mercy and a trust rather than a prize?
